title: The Diamond Sutra, Part I
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan's talk emphasizes the importance of letting go of attachments and perceptions of a self when giving gifts or engaging in generosity. This means not creating mental labels or concepts about objects or attributes, but instead allowing them to be given freely without attachment. By doing so, we can accumulate infinite merit and gain clarity of mind, ultimately leading to liberation from suffering.

sentences.text: **Seiu Hannah Sullivan:** *Thus have I heard.
Once the Bhagavan was dwelling near Shravasti at Anapinadatta Garden in Jetav Forest together with a full assembly of 1,250 bhikshus and a great many fearless bodhisattvas.
One day before noon the Bhagavan put on his patched robe, picked up his bowl and entered the capital of Shravasti for offerings.
After begging for food in the city and eating his meal of rice, he returned from his daily round in the afternoon, put on his robe and bowl away, washed his feet and sat down on the appointed seat.
After crossing his legs and adjusting his body, he turned his awareness to what was before him.*
*A number of bhikshus then came up to where the Bhagavan was sitting.
After touching their heads to his feet, they walked around him to the right three times and sat down to one side.
On this occasion, the Venerable Sabhuti was also present in the assembly.
Rising from his seat, he uncovered one shoulder and touched his right knee to the ground.

Pressing his palms together and bowing to the Buddha, he said, "It is rare, Bhagavan, most rare indeed, Sugata, how the Tathagata, the Arhan, the fully enlightened one, blesses fearless bodhisattvas with the best of blessings.
And it is rare, Bhagavan, how the Tathagata, the Arhan, the fully enlightened one, entrusts fearless bodhisattvas with the greatest of trusts.
Even so, Bhagavan, if a noble son or daughter should set forth on the bodhisattva path, how should they stand, how should they walk, and how should they control their thoughts?"*

*The Buddha told the Venerable Sabhuti, "Well said, Sabhuti, well said, so it is, Sabhuti, it is as you say, the Tathagata blesses fearless bodhisattvas with the best of blessings and entrusts fearless bodhisattvas with the greatest of trusts.
You should therefore truly listen, Sabhuti, and consider this well.
I shall tell you how those who set forth on the bodhisattva path should stand, how they should walk, and how they should control their thoughts."
The Venerable Sabhuti answered, "May it be so, Bhagavan," and gave his full attention.
The Buddha said to him, "Sabhuti, those who would now set forth on the bodhisattva path should thus give birth to this thought.

However many beings there are, in whatever realms of being might exist, whether they are born from an egg or born from a womb, born from the water or born from the air, whether they have form or no form, whether they have perception or no perception, or neither perception nor no perception, in whatever conceivable realm of being one might conceive of beings, in the realm of complete nirvana, I shall liberate them all.
And though I thus liberate countless beings, not a single being is liberated.
And why not, Sabhuti, a bodhisattva who creates the perception of a being cannot be called a bodhisattva?*
*And why not, Sabhuti, no one can be called a bodhisattva who creates the perception of a self, or who creates the perception of a being, a life, or a soul?
Moreover, Sabhuti, when bodhisattvas give a gift, they should not be attached to a thing.
When they give a gift, they should not be attached to anything at all.
They should not be attached to a sight when they give a gift, nor should they be attached to a sound, a smell, a taste, a touch, or a dharma when they give a gift.
Thus, Sabhuti, fearless bodhisattvas should give a gift without being attached to the perception of an object.
And why?
Sabhuti, the body of merit of those bodhisattvas who give a gift without being attached is not easy to measure."*
*"What do you think, Sabhuti?
Is the space to the east easy to measure?"
And Sabhuti replied, "No, it is not, Bhagavan."
The Buddha said, "Likewise is the space to the south, to the west, to the north, in between, above, below, or in any of the ten directions, easy to measure?"
Sabhuti replied, "No, it is not, Bhagavan."
The Buddha said, "So it is, Sabhuti.
The body of merit of those bodhisattvas who give a gift without being attached is not easy to measure.
Thus, Sabhuti, those who set forth on the bodhisattva path should give a gift without being attached to the perception of an object.
What do you think, Sabhuti?
Can the Tathagata be seen by means of the possession of attributes?"*
*Sabhuti replied, "No, indeed, Bhagavan.
The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the possession of attributes.
And why not?
Bhagavan, what the Tathagata says is the possession of attributes, is no possession of attributes."

This having been said, the Buddha told the venerable Sabhuti, "Since the possession of attributes is an illusion, Sabhuti, and no possession of attributes is no illusion, by means of attributes that are no attributes, the Tathagata can indeed be seen."

Thus having been said, this having been said, the venerable Sabhuti asked the Buddha, "Bhagavan, will there be any beings in the future, in the final epoch, in the final period, in the final 500 years of the Dharma-ending age, who give birth to a perception of the truth of the words of a sutra, such as that spoken here?"*

*The Buddha said, "Sabhuti, do not ask, will there be any beings in the future, in the final epoch, in the final period, in the final 500 years of the Dharma-ending age, who give birth to a perception of the truth of the words of a sutra, such as that spoken here?

Surely, Sabhuti, in the future, in the final epoch, in the final period, in the final 500 years of the Dharma-ending age, there will be fearless bodhisattvas who are capable, virtuous, and wise, who give birth to a perception of the truth of the words of a sutra, such as that spoken here?
Indeed, Sabhuti, such fearless bodhisattvas will have honored not just one Buddha, and they will have planted auspicious roots before not just one Buddha.

Surely, Sabhuti, such fearless bodhisattvas will have honored countless hundreds and thousands of Buddhas, and they will have planted auspicious roots before countless hundreds and thousands of Buddhas."*
*"In the words of a sutra, such as that spoken here, they are sure to gain perfect clarity of mind.
The Tathagata knows them, Sabhuti, by means of his Buddha knowledge, and the Tathagata sees him, Sabhuti, by means of his Buddha vision.
The Tathagata is aware of them, Sabhuti, for they all produce and receive a measureless, infinite body of merit.
And how so?
Because, Sabhuti, these fearless bodhisattvas do not create the perception of a self, nor do they create the perception of a being, a life, or a soul.
Nor, Sabhuti, do these fearless bodhisattvas create the perception of a dharma, much less the perception of no dharma.
Sabhuti, they do not create a perception, nor no perception.
And why not?
Because, Sabhuti, if these fearless bodhisattvas created the perception of a dharma, they would be attached to a self, a being, a life, and a soul.
Likewise, if they created the perception of no dharma, they would be attached to a self, a being, a life, and a soul.
And why not?
Because, surely, Sabhuti, fearless bodhisattvas do not cling to a dharma, much less to no dharma.*
*This is the meaning behind the Tathagata's saying, 'A dharma teaching is like a raft.' If you should let go of dharmas, how much more so?
No dharmas."*
So, for this practice period, we're looking at the Diamond Sutra.
Let me just say that as far as mastery goes, we are all in this together.
I'm not the expert here, but I vow to hold the space for mutual exploration throughout this practice period.
Also known as the Vajracchidika Prajnaparamita Sutra, or the Sutra that cuts through illusion, it's been called the oldest existing piece of literature, printed piece of literature.
That document is dated May 11th, 1868 A.D.
It lives at the British Library, and it looks like the photo on our class advertisement, and we'll look at that in greater depth at another time.
The document itself was published with the intention of being distributed, free of charge, to all those who wished to read it.
But hey, this is getting ahead of itself.
What were people doing, thinking, 2000 years ago?
The teachings themselves began at the time of Shakyamuni Buddha, approximately 400 BCE, strictly through oral transmission.
It was in verse, with lots of repetition, helpful in memorization, so as to be passed on.
I think we all studied Greek mythology in school and learned about the wandering troubadours who transmitted the teachings of the gods and goddesses.
The Diamond Sutra was taught that way, with lots of repetition, so that people could remember it.
It's part of the next step in the emptiness teachings, which was Buddha's early message to the Prajnaparamita Sutras and the development of Mahayana Buddhism.
These include a long incarnation of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in 8,000 lines, which expanded and contracted up to 100,000 lines, and down to perhaps the most compact, our beloved Heart Sutra.
Scholars disagree, but there's evidence to suggest the Diamond Sutra came first, not after all of those Perfection Wisdom offerings.
I chose the Diamond Sutra because I had never read it, and I had been studying the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 lines, translated by Edward Kansi.
So it was on my list.
The first time I read it, I was in turn charmed, befuddled, and confused, and exalted by the verse, numbed by the density and the repetition.
Of course, I immediately jumped into the commentaries to try to make sense of it.

Our primary text offered by Red Pine is full of options, as he does his own commentaries, and includes pearls from at least nine scholars, including Vasubandhu, who I like to remember for his reference to storehouse consciousness, and Huineng, the sixth patriarch, the ancestor whom we so often meet in Dharma talks.

Legend says Huineng was an illiterate woodcutter who heard a passerby reciting the Diamond Sutra, as was a common practice in China at that time, and was so galvanized that he walked out of his former life into the monastic setting, where eventually he became the sixth patriarch.
However, I urge us to follow the advice of Thich Nhat Hanh, at least in the beginning of reading the Sutra.
He says:
*"The Sutra is so deep and wonderful.
It has its own language.
Late at night, it's a pleasure to recite the Diamond Sutra alone, in complete silence.
Its language seems mysterious, but when you look deeply, you can understand.
Don't rush into the commentaries, or you may be unduly influenced by them.
Please read the Sutra first.
You may see things that no commentator has seen.
You can read as if you were chanting, using your clear body and mind to be in touch with the words.
Try to understand the Sutra from your own experiences and your own suffering.
It is helpful to ask, do these teachings of the Buddha have anything to do with my daily life?
Abstract ideas can be beautiful, but if they have nothing to do with our life, of what use are they?
So please ask, do the words have anything to do with eating a meal, drinking tea, cutting wood, or carrying water?"*
The Sutra begins with a formal opening, "Thus have I heard."
This is to ascribe it to Shakyamuni Buddha's words.
The formal questioning posture introduces Subhuti, our other main character, besides Shakyamuni Buddha himself.
Subhuti is an Arhat, one who has advanced in the path of enlightenment.
Bended knee, right shoulder bared, palms together: this image is the formal questioning posture.
So I guess we should ask our teachers if this should be our new dokusan posture.
He asks how we should practice.
So a scene is set for outlining the foundation of Mahayana Buddhism.
In verse three, the idea of a self, no self, is approached for the first time.
The Buddha says, "However many beings there are in whatever many realms may exist, I shall liberate them all.
And though I thus liberate countless beings, not a single being is liberated.
No one can call themselves a bodhisattva who creates the perception of a self or creates the perception of a being, a life, or a soul."
This is the deep message of the Buddha, no self.
Does it mean that we have no self?
The key, I think, here is the perception of a self.
We go around thinking about ourselves all the time, from "I can tie my shoe" to "I am a doctor," or "I am afraid," or "I am going to die."
We are always looking at our favorite subject, myself.
Of course, there is someone who is tying the shoe, or it wouldn't get tied.
The I, who is a doctor, has spent years and millions of brain cells getting to the title of doctor.
It's just that we start out on a spiral, leading potentially to "How great is it that I just tied my shoe," "I am a doctor," and by the way, "What makes me different, better, less than?"
What?
Whom?
It isn't really about the shoe or the vocation.
It's about the perception we developed about ourselves relative to the object and about others relative to our perception.
So if we really want to be a bodhisattva, we can't pin a metal on ourselves for our good deeds because we are digging ourselves into the whole of the perception of self, independent of other.
In verse four, the idea of gift giving arises.
This is a favorite of mine because I love the meal chant: *May we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift.*
I see this in my own life as a safety check around that old devil's self.
If I give a donation to a worthy cause, will I feel superior about my own standing economically relative to the recipients of the gift?
If I give a coat to someone who doesn't have one, will I feel sorry for them because they didn't have a coat?
If I find the perfect blanket for my granddaughter, will I hold on to wanting her to like it?
Can I give a gift without being attached to the outcome?
In verse six, even the teachings are on the chopping block.
We are given the teachings as a raft.
